draft.title: Multi-locale overflow audit: a computable clip/wrap detector for de/en/fr/it
draft.principle_summary: Two separable claims. (1) The WCAG 1.4.4/1.4.10 family (T1, formal standard) already gives Solen a working DEFINITION of "overflow failure": content that gets clipped, truncated, obscured, or that overlaps another element when the rendered text grows, is a failure regardless of cause. The same DOM-diffing test used for a 200% zoom check works unchanged for a locale swap, because both are "make the string longer and see if the box breaks." (2) The widely-cited IBM/W3C length-dependent expansion table (T3, vendor data republished by W3C, not a controlled study) says the RIGHT test strings are not the English draft but a synthetic worst-case string sized by expansion bucket: under 10 chars can hit 200-300%, 11-20 chars roughly 180-200%, 21-30 roughly 160-180%, 31-50 roughly 140-160%, 51-70 roughly 151-170% (note: this bucket is not monotonically below the 31-50 bucket in IBM's own published table, which is itself a sign the table is empirical folklore, not a formula), over 70 roughly 130%. Solen already has the correct honest tier on this exact number (RATIONALE.md:206 cites it as T3-equivalent, "round-2 delta"), and separately keeps a flat 20-35% range for sentence-scale copy (RATIONALE.md:130, RATIONALE.md:197). Neither figure is a measured fact about Solen's own de/en/fr/it strings; both are inherited industry heuristics used as PLANNING buckets, not as a verified pass/fail threshold. The gap this stream closes is not re-deriving the expansion number (that is S33's job, cross-referenced), it is building the instrument that would make the number obsolete: measure Solen's OWN four locale files directly, per string, per surface, and flag overflow against the real rendered container rather than trusting any inherited percentage at all.

sources.claim: WCAG 2.1 Success Criterion 1.4.4 (Resize Text) requires content not to be clipped, truncated, or obscured when text is resized up to 200%; overflow:hidden on a fixed-width container is a named failure mode (Technique F69).
sources.source: W3C, Understanding SC 1.4.4 Resize Text (w3.org/WAI/WCAG21/Understanding/resize-text) and Technique F69 (w3.org/TR/WCAG20-TECHS/F69.html)

sources.claim: WCAG 2.1 Success Criterion 1.4.10 (Reflow) requires no loss of content/functionality at 400% zoom equivalent (320 CSS px viewport); this is the stricter sibling test and the standard the D9 injected-viewport pass should target for the audit's zoom axis.

IBM's Guidelines to design global solutions publish an expansion-by-source-length table: <=10 chars 200-300%, 11-20 chars 180-200%, 21-30 chars 160-180%, 31-50 chars 140-160%, 51-70 chars 151-170%, >70 chars 130%.
sources.source: W3C Internationalization Activity, 'Text size in translation' (w3.org/International/articles/article-text-size.en.html), explicitly crediting IBM as the data source, not W3C original research

sources.claim: German UI strings commonly run 20-35% longer than English at sentence scale, with short labels able to double in length, driven by compound nouns (e.g. 'Input processing features' to 'Eingabeverarbeitungsfunktionen').
sources.source: W3C Internationalization Activity, 'Text size in translation' (same article); this is the same IBM-derived vendor heuristic, not a separate study

sources.claim: German compound words do not line-wrap at spaces the way English does; without hyphens:auto plus a correct lang attribute, a long compound either overflows its container or forces an ugly mid-word break.
sources.source: General CSS/typography behavior of German orthography (no spaces inside compounds); documented in the same W3C i18n article as a wrapping failure example

draft.solen_current: RATIONALE.md section 9 (lines 193-208) already covers the MECHANICS well and already tiers the expansion number honestly: line 197 gives the CONV-tiered flat 20-35% sentence-scale range; line 206 gives the T3-tiered length-dependent bucket table (correctly citing W3C/IBM, correctly flagging it as a heuristic); line 248's folklore table explicitly kills the unsourced flat "30 percent" from SOURCE.md:1075 and tells the reader to treat it as a range or measure Solen's own strings. RATIONALE.md line 199 already names three concrete German/French overflow test strings (Terminbestätigung, Haarverlängerung, Wegbeschreibung, Renseignements complémentaires) and states the design rule (size fixed-width slots against the longest locale, not the EN draft). LOCKFILE.md around line 765 locks the <=3-word CTA rule as the mitigation. The gap register at RATIONALE.md:847 already names this exact stream as D9 ("Multi-locale overflow audit: render de/en/fr/it, flag clipped/wrapped CTAs and chips") and marks it Mechanizable = YES, i.e. Solen's own audit already knows this test should exist and has not built it. GEOMETRY_PRINCIPLES_2026-07-17.md:760 independently proposes the exact same instrument shape ("inject a stylesheet forcing WCAG 1.4.12 spacing ratios onto any page and check for clipped/overlapping/hidden content, a scriptable pass/fail test") for a neighboring failure mode (forced text-spacing), confirming this is a reusable pattern, not a one-off. `npm run exists "locale overflow"` returns zero hits: no such script exists in the repo today. messages/{de,en,fr,it}.json hold the four locale string files; scripts/mcp/site-tester already gives Solen a local Playwright driver that could host this pass.
draft.gap: RATIONALE.md documents the MECHANICS (why overflow happens, which rule mitigates it, an honestly-tiered expansion heuristic) but has no COMPUTABLE METRIC: no defined inputs, no formula, no threshold, no output shape. D9 sits in the gap register as "YES, mechanizable" but unbuilt. This stream's job is to specify that metric (inputs/formula/thresholds/output), not to touch the already-honest tiering of the expansion percentage itself (that stays as RATIONALE.md already has it, cross-ref S33).
draft.proposed_addition:
COMPUTABLE METRIC SPEC: Multi-locale overflow audit (D9)

PURPOSE: flag any DOM element whose rendered box clips, wraps unexpectedly compared to its EN baseline, or overlaps a sibling once the surface renders in de/fr/it instead of en. Answers "which locale breaks this screen" with element-level coordinates, not a vibe.

INPUTS:
1. A list of target routes/surfaces (start with the D9 gap register's own examples: any screen carrying CTAs, chips, tabs, badges; pull the route list from the same crawl.mjs route enumeration site-tester already uses for test-sweep).
2. The four locale builds: render each route at locale=de, en, fr, it via the existing Next.js i18n routing (no new infra: /de/..., /en/..., /fr/..., /it/...).
3. Three fixed viewport widths per WCAG-aligned test matrix: 375px (mobile, primary), 768px (tablet), 1280px (desktop) at 100% zoom; OPTIONAL fourth pass at 320px CSS width to align with the WCAG 1.4.10 reflow standard (T1) if the audit wants a stricter mode.
4. Per-element capture set: every node matching a fixed-width or single-line-intent selector class already in the design system: button/CTA (`.rounded-full` interactive, any `<button>`), TabPill, chip/badge, table/column header, nav label. Skip free-flowing body/paragraph blocks, they are explicitly out of scope for D9 (that is domain 4's measure/line-length concern, already covered).

FORMULA (per element, per locale, per viewport):
- Capture `getBoundingClientRect()` and `scrollWidth`/`clientWidth`, `scrollHeight`/`clientHeight` for the element AND its immediate parent container, in EN (baseline) and in the target locale (de/fr/it).
- CLIP flag: `scrollWidth > clientWidth` OR `scrollHeight > clientHeight` on the element itself (native overflow, matches WCAG Technique F69's definition directly, T1-grounded).
- WRAP-DELTA flag: element `rect.height` in the target locale > baseline EN `rect.height` by more than one computed line-height (i.e. the element grew a line it did not have in EN). Single-line-intent elements (buttons, pills, tabs) flag on ANY height growth; multi-line-tolerant elements (card titles) flag only past +1 line.
- OVERLAP flag: for elements sharing a row/flex container, target-locale bounding boxes intersect where the EN baseline boxes did not (sibling collision from a swollen neighbor).
- CONTAINER-BREACH flag: element `rect.right` exceeds parent `clientWidth` bound (element pushed outside its intended slot without native scroll overflow, e.g. flex items that got compressed to 0 or negative-margin escapes).

THRESHOLDS (what counts as a reportable failure vs noise):
- CLIP and OVERLAP: always report (binary, WCAG-grounded, zero tolerance per the T1 standard).
- WRAP-DELTA on single-line-intent elements: always report (this is exactly the CTA-wrap failure LOCKFILE:765's 3-word rule exists to prevent).
- WRAP-DELTA on multi-line-tolerant elements: report only if the container-relative used-height ratio exceeds a length-bucket-scaled tolerance. Since the source string length varies per element, apply the T3 IBM bucket as the EXPECTED ceiling, not a strict threshold: an element whose target-locale string is under 10 EN characters is allowed up to +200% length before flagging; 11-30 chars up to +180%; 31-70 chars up to +150%; over 70 chars up to +130%. A flag fires only when actual rendered growth exceeds the bucket's OWN ceiling, meaning the audit treats the IBM number as a permissive upper bound for triage, not as ground truth (correct T3 usage: use it to sort signal from noise, do not treat its magnitude as verified).

OUTPUT SHAPE: one row per (route, element selector/testid, locale, viewport) with the four boolean flags, the EN and locale-string values, the two bounding rects, and a computed severity: CLIP or OVERLAP = blocking (matches WCAG failure, ships nothing); WRAP-DELTA past bucket ceiling on interactive elements = high; WRAP-DELTA within bucket but visually notable (any flag at all on a multi-line-tolerant block) = informational. Sort blocking first. This is the same severity split D10 already proposes generically (contract breach = blocking regardless of size, within-budget = cosmetic); D9's output should slot into that shared severity vocabulary rather than invent its own.

BUILD NOTE (not code, just the shape): implement as a site-tester crawl variant, reusing crawl.mjs's route enumeration and Playwright session, looping locale x viewport x route, running one `page.evaluate()` per route that walks the interactive-element selector list and returns the rect/scroll data as JSON, diffed against a cached EN baseline pass. No new dependency; this is measurement plumbing on infra the repo already has (site-tester), plus messages/{de,fr,it}.json as the string source of truth.

WHAT THIS DOES NOT DO: it does not re-derive or re-verify the IBM expansion percentages as facts about German or French generally (that verification, if ever needed, is S33's job against academic/localization-industry sources). It uses the T3 number only as a triage ceiling for noise reduction, explicitly labeled as such, so a future correction to the underlying percentage only changes the tolerance dial, not the instrument's correctness (CLIP/OVERLAP/CONTAINER-BREACH stay T1-grounded and threshold-free regardless).

TASTE-LAB PROBE (only if the owner wants to hand-calibrate the WRAP-DELTA bucket tolerances rather than trust IBM's table wholesale): run the audit once against the three named test strings already in RATIONALE.md:199 (Terminbestätigung, Haarverlängerung, Wegbeschreibung, Renseignements complémentaires) on their real call-sites, show the owner the actual before/after screenshots side by side with the flag verdicts, and ask a single binary per flagged element: "does this read as broken, yes or no." Four to six elements is enough to sanity-check whether the IBM-derived ceilings are too strict (flagging fine wraps) or too loose (missing an actual break) for Solen's own type scale and container widths, without needing a full academic re-derivation.
draft.taste_lab_probe: Render the three RATIONALE.md:199 test strings (Terminbestätigung, Haarverlängerung, Wegbeschreibung, plus FR Renseignements complementaires) at their real call sites, screenshot EN vs the target locale side by side, run the proposed CLIP/WRAP-DELTA/OVERLAP flags against each, and ask the owner one binary judgment per flagged element (broken, yes or no) to calibrate whether the IBM-derived bucket ceilings are too strict or too loose for Solen's actual type scale, before trusting the ceilings at full scale across all routes.

verified.residual_risks: Not a claim failure but a real inconsistency worth flagging to the owner as a QUESTIONS.md / RATIONALE.md correction candidate: RATIONALE.md line 206 (existing, pre-dates this stream) paraphrases the IBM/W3C expansion table incorrectly. Verified against the live W3C source, the real table is <=10 chars 200-300%, 11-20 chars 180-200%, 21-30 chars 160-180%, 31-50 chars 140-160%, 51-70 chars 151-170%, >70 chars 130%. RATIONALE.md:206 instead says "11-20 chars roughly 80-100, 21-70 chars roughly 40, 71+ roughly 30" which does not match the source it cites and looks like a transcription error (possibly a dropped leading digit: 180-200 -> 80-100). This draft's own sources[] table and its proposed threshold buckets both use the CORRECT figures, so the new addition is internally accurate, but the draft's solen_current narrative overstates how "correct" the existing RATIONALE.md:206 text already is. Recommend a follow-up one-line fix to RATIONALE.md:206 itself (out of this stream's stated scope, cross-ref S33) rather than silently leaving two different versions of the same cited table in the same file. Separately, the flat 20-35% CONV figure at RATIONALE.md:197 remains unverified industry folklore as RATIONALE.md itself already discloses; this stream correctly does not lean on it for the new metric's thresholds.

claim_verdicts.claim: WCAG 2.1 SC 1.4.4 (Resize Text) requires content not be clipped, truncated, or obscured at 200% resize; Technique F69 is the named failure mode.
claim_verdicts.note: Verified live against w3.org/WAI/WCAG21/Understanding/resize-text.html. The page explicitly names F69 and describes exactly this clip/truncate/obscure failure. Tier T1 holds.

claim_verdicts.claim: WCAG 2.1 SC 1.4.10 (Reflow) requires no loss of content/functionality at 400% zoom equivalent (320 CSS px viewport).
claim_verdicts.note: Standard, well-documented WCAG success criterion; the URL and mechanism (320px CSS reflow viewport) are the correct, real description. Not independently re-fetched but this is settled public spec text, not a contested figure.

claim_verdicts.claim: IBM's expansion-by-source-length table: <=10 chars 200-300%, 11-20 chars 180-200%, 21-30 chars 160-180%, 31-50 chars 140-160%, 51-70 chars 151-170%, >70 chars 130%.
claim_verdicts.note: Verified live via WebFetch against w3.org/International/articles/article-text-size.en.html. The table matches exactly, including the non-monotonic 51-70 bucket. Correctly tiered T3 (vendor data republished by W3C, not a controlled study) by the draft.

claim_verdicts.claim: German/French UI strings commonly run 20-35% longer than English at sentence scale, short labels can double.
claim_verdicts.note: The W3C article gives specific WORKED EXAMPLES (e.g. 'Input processing features' -> 'Eingabeverarbeitungsfunktionen', a single word expanding 2.8x) but does NOT publish a blanket 20-35% sentence-scale percentage anywhere I could confirm in the fetched content. RATIONALE.md itself already flags the flat-30% version of this claim as unsourced folklore (line 248) and downgrades it to a CONV range. The draft correctly treats this as inherited industry heuristic and does not lean on it for the new metric's thresholds, so it does not weaken the deliverable, but the magnitude itself remains unverified beyond RATIONALE's own honest caveat.

claim_verdicts.claim: German compound words do not line-wrap at spaces; without hyphens:auto plus lang attribute, a long compound overflows or forces a mid-word break.
claim_verdicts.note: General, well-established CSS/orthography behavior (German compounds lack internal spaces), consistent with the W3C article's own wrapping example. Reasonable T2, not overclaimed as T1.

claim_verdicts.claim: GEOMETRY_PRINCIPLES_2026-07-17.md:760 proposes the same instrument shape (inject a stylesheet, check for clipped/overlapping/hidden content) for WCAG 1.4.12 text-spacing.
claim_verdicts.note: Confirmed by direct grep: line 760 reads exactly as described, and line 759 cites the real W3C Understanding SC 1.4.12 page. Precedent claim holds.

claim_verdicts.claim: RATIONALE.md section 9 (lines 193-208) already covers the mechanics and already correctly tiers the length-dependent expansion table (T3, correctly citing W3C/IBM).
claim_verdicts.note: Read directly. RATIONALE.md:206 exists and does cite 'W3C Text size in translation restating IBM globalization data' but the NUMBERS IT GIVES ('11-20 chars roughly 80-100, 21-70 chars roughly 40, 71+ roughly 30') do not match the real IBM/W3C table verified above (180-200%, 160-180/140-160/151-170%, 130%). This looks like a pre-existing transcription error in RATIONALE.md, not something introduced by this draft. The draft's claim that RATIONALE.md 'already gives the correct T3-tiered bucket table' is therefore not accurate as stated; the draft's OWN proposed_addition uses the verified-correct numbers, so the new content is not compromised, but the solen_current framing oversells the existing file's accuracy. Recorded in residual_risks as a correction candidate rather than silently fixed here (out of this stream's stated scope).
